answer.label: Not William Shakespeare — a traditional Yiddish proverb
answer.authorDates: Traditional Ashkenazi Jewish saying · author unknown
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in none of Shakespeare’s plays, poems, or letters. It is documented across reference works as a Yiddish (Jewish) proverb — anonymous folk wisdom — and Wikiquote files it under Shakespeare’s “Misattributed” sayings. No early edition pins the exact English wording, so it is best treated as a traditional proverb, not a Shakespeare quotation.

source.heading: A folk proverb, not a line from the plays

source.excerpt: When a father gives to his son, both laugh; when a son gives to his father, both cry.
trail: Searchable concordances of the complete works return no match; the anti-misattribution project “Not By Shakespeare” reviews the line and concludes “it’s not Shakespeare,” finding only references to a “Jewish proverb” (Shakespeare Geek / Not By Shakespeare).
Wikiquote lists the exact line in its William Shakespeare “Misattributed” section, noting it is “attributed in English sources as a Yiddish proverb.”
Quotation databases that name an author credit an anonymous “Yiddish Proverb,” not Shakespeare — consistent with the folk-saying origin.
source.excerptNote: The saying circulates in near-identical form as a Yiddish/Jewish proverb, sometimes rendered “… both weep” for the second clause.
source.rightsNote: This is an anonymous traditional proverb: no single author and no first-publication edition can be tied to the exact English wording, so no copyright status can be asserted. The underlying folk saying is old and unowned, but a particular modern printed translation could itself be under copyright — we make no public-domain claim for a specific rendering we cannot source.

author.name: Yiddish proverb tradition
author.heading: Anonymous Jewish folk wisdom
author.metaLine: Traditional Ashkenazi Jewish saying · author unknown
author.bio: Yiddish proverbs are the distilled folk wisdom of Ashkenazi Jewish communities of Central and Eastern Europe, carried orally over centuries before being gathered into printed collections. This saying captures a bittersweet truth about the generations: a parent gives to a child joyfully, while a grown child giving back to an aging parent carries an ache of role-reversal. Like most proverbs it has no known individual author — and no connection to Shakespeare.

misattribution.heading: Why Shakespeare gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Feel-good, aphoristic lines gravitate toward famous names, and Shakespeare is the single biggest magnet for “wise-sounding” quotes in English. This proverb’s polished antithesis sounds Shakespearean, so it was pinned on him — but it is a folk saying he never wrote.

items.why: The line is in none of the plays, poems, or sonnets, and Wikiquote catalogues it in Shakespeare’s “Misattributed” section. Quote-image sites nonetheless mass-produce it over his name.

Reference works and quotation databases consistently label it a Yiddish / Jewish proverb of unknown authorship — occasionally also cited as a Serbian proverb, underscoring that it is unowned folk wisdom rather than one writer’s line.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no primary Shakespeare source because he did not write it: the line is a traditional Yiddish proverb, as the Not By Shakespeare project and Wikiquote both find.

context.heading: What the proverb means
lead: The saying turns on a single reversal. A father giving to his son is the natural order — provision flowing downward, forward into the future — and so “both laugh.” A son giving to his father inverts that order: it usually means the father can no longer provide for himself, that age and dependence have arrived, and so “both cry.” The joy and the grief spring from the same act of giving, pointed in opposite directions across the generations.
This bittersweet, hard-earned wisdom is exactly the register of Yiddish folk proverbs — which is why it reads as ancient and true, and why it never needed a Shakespeare to have said it.
context.pull: Provision flowing forward is joy; provision flowing back is loss.
